The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(\mathsf X,\Sigma_X)$, $(\mathsf Y,\Sigma_Y)$, and $(\mathsf A,\Sigma_A)$ be nonempty measurable spaces. A **source/target pair of joint laws** consists of probability measures $P_S$ and $P_T$ on $(\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y,\Sigma_X\otimes\Sigma_Y)$. For $D\in\{S,T\}$, its input marginal is the probability measure $\mu_D$ on $(\mathsf X,\Sigma_X)$ defined by $\mu_D(A)=P_D(A\times\mathsf Y)$. If $h:\mathsf X\to\mathsf A$ is measurable and $\ell:\mathsf A\times\mathsf Y\to[0,+\infty]$ is product-measurable, then $(x,y)\mapsto(h(x),y)$ is measurable: the preimage of a measurable rectangle $U\times V$ is $h^{-1}(U)\times V$, and such rectangles generate the product sigma-algebra. Taking preimages once more shows that $(x,y)\mapsto\ell(h(x),y)$ is measurable. The domain risk is the extended nonnegative integral
$$R_D(h):=\int_{\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y}\ell(h(x),y)\,P_D(d(x,y)).$$

A **conditional label kernel** for $P_D$ is a specified probability kernel $K_D$ from $(\mathsf X,\Sigma_X)$ to $(\mathsf Y,\Sigma_Y)$ such that, for every nonnegative product-measurable $g:\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y\to[0,+\infty]$,
$$\int g(x,y)\,P_D(d(x,y))=\int_{\mathsf X}\left(\int_{\mathsf Y}g(x,y)\,K_D(x,dy)\right)\mu_D(dx).$$
The pair is under **covariate shift** when conditional label kernels $K_S,K_T$ are supplied, there is a measurable set $N$ with $\mu_T(N)=0$ such that $K_S(x,\cdot)=K_T(x,\cdot)$ as probability measures for every $x\notin N$, and $\mu_T\ll\mu_S$. No existence of conditional kernels is asserted by this definition.

Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be dominated by the fixed sigma-finite positive measure $\mu$. For each
$\theta$, the Radon–Nikodym theorem gives the almost-everywhere class
$dP_\theta/d\mu$; a sigma-finite exhaustion for $\mu$ is also finite for the
probability measure $P_\theta$. Under AC, select simultaneously a
finite-valued measurable nonnegative representative $p_\theta$ from each
class. The nonnegative version exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].

For fixed observed $x\in\mathcal X$, the function
$$L_x:\Theta\to[0,+\infty),\qquad L_x(\theta):=p_\theta(x),$$
is the **likelihood at $x$**. This is a function on the parameter labels, not
a probability distribution on $\Theta$. No sigma-algebra on $\Theta$ or
measurability of $L_x$ is implied. Each density is determined only
$\mu$-almost everywhere; there is no canonical pointwise version and, for
arbitrary uncountable $\Theta$, no common exceptional null set is asserted.

Let $P_0$ and $P_1$ be probability measures on the same measurable space.
Assume AC. Their Lebesgue decomposition relative to $P_0$ is the unique
decomposition
$P_1=P_{1,\mathrm{ac}}+P_{1,\mathrm{s}}$ with
$P_{1,\mathrm{ac}}\ll P_0$ and $P_{1,\mathrm{s}}\perp P_0$
([[thm-lebesgue-decomposition-exists-for-sigma-finite-signed-measures]],
[[thm-lebesgue-decomposition-is-unique-for-sigma-finite-signed-measures]]).
Both components are positive by
[[lem-positive-lebesgue-components-of-a-positive-measure]], and
$P_{1,\mathrm{ac}}$ is finite because their sum has mass one. Define the
**likelihood-ratio density** of $P_1$ against $P_0$ to be the
$P_0$-almost-everywhere class
$$
\frac{dP_{1,\mathrm{ac}}}{dP_0}
$$
of [[def-radon-nikodym-derivative]]. Under AC this class has a nonnegative
measurable representative by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].

This is a full density of $P_1$ with respect to $P_0$ only in the
absolutely continuous case $P_1\ll P_0$. If that condition fails, the
singular component remains separate. A displayed representative is not a
canonical pointwise function: its values are determined only
$P_0$-almost everywhere.

Assume AC and let $P_0,P_1$ be probability measures on one measurable space.
Let $r$ be a nonnegative measurable representative of the likelihood-ratio
class for $P_1$ versus $P_0$. If $P_1\ll P_0$, then
$$
E_{P_0}[g r]=E_{P_1}[g]
$$
for every nonnegative measurable $g$, and also for every real-valued
$P_1$-integrable measurable $g$. Here $E_{P_i}[h]$ means
$\int h\,dP_i$. Without $P_1\ll P_0$, this identity need not hold because the
singular component may be nonzero.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. The **measure with density $f$ relative
to $\mu$** is the measure
$$f\,d\mu:\mathcal A\to[0,+\infty],\qquad (f\,d\mu)(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu,$$
whose measure property is supplied by
[[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]].

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ and $(Y,\mathcal{B})$ be measurable spaces
([[def-measurable-space]]). A function $f : X \to Y$ is **measurable** when

$$f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \qquad \text{for every } B \in \mathcal{B}.$$

Equivalently, the family

$$\mathcal{C}_f := \{\, B \subseteq Y : f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \,\}$$

is a sigma-algebra on $Y$ containing $\mathcal{B}$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

1. If $f,g:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ are measurable and $f+g$ is defined
   pointwise, then $f+g$ is measurable.
2. If $c\in\mathbb R$ and $f:X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable, then $cf$ is
   measurable.
3. If $f:X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable, then $f^+=\max\{f,0\}$,
   $f^-=\max\{-f,0\}$, and $|f|=f^++f^-$ are measurable.
4. If $E\in\mathcal A$ and $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, then
   $f\chi_E$ is measurable, where this function equals $f$ on $E$ and $0$
   off $E$ (in particular, $0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ here).
5. If $(f_n)$ is a sequence of measurable functions $X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$,
   then $\inf_n f_n$ is measurable; if moreover $f_n\uparrow f$ pointwise, then
   $f$ is measurable.

Let $X$ be a set. A **pi-system on $X$** is a nonempty family
$\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal P(X)$ closed under binary intersections: if
$A,B\in\mathcal P$, then $A\cap B\in\mathcal P$.

The nonempty-family requirement is the convention used here. It does not require
$X\in\mathcal P$ and it does not add an empty-intersection axiom.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$ and let $\mathcal A=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. If finite measures $\mu$ and $
u$ on $(X,\mathcal A)$ agree on $\mathcal P$ and satisfy $\mu(X)=
u(X)$, then $\mu=
u$ on $\mathcal A$.

The total-mass equality is separate because this library's pi-system convention does not require $X\in\mathcal P$.

Let $(\mathsf X,\Sigma_X)$, $(\mathsf Y,\Sigma_Y)$, and $(\mathsf A,\Sigma_A)$ be nonempty measurable spaces. A **source/target pair of joint laws** consists of probability measures $P_S$ and $P_T$ on $(\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y,\Sigma_X\otimes\Sigma_Y)$. Taking preimages once more shows that $(x,y)\mapsto\ell(h(x),y)$ is measurable. The domain risk is the extended nonnegative integral

The pair is under **covariate shift** when conditional label kernels $K_S,K_T$ are supplied, there is a measurable set $N$ with $\mu_T(N)=0$ such that $K_S(x,\cdot)=K_T(x,\cdot)$ as probability measures for every $x\notin N$, and $\mu_T\ll\mu_S$. No existence of conditional kernels is asserted by this definition.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $E$ be measurable with $\mu(E)=0$.
Then
$$\int_E f\,d\mu=0.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

The middle equality uses the $\mu_T$-almost-everywhere equality of the specified kernels, and the last equality uses their target disintegration [F1].

The measurable rectangles form the generating $\pi$-system in [F7], so [F8] and steps 1.1–1.2 give $\nu_0=P_T$ on the entire product sigma-algebra. By [F2], there is a measurable $N\in\Sigma_X$ with $\mu_S(N)=0$ outside of which $w=w_0$. By [F14], $P_S(N\times\mathsf Y)=0$. derivations.claim: Set $g_h(x,y):=\ell(h(x),y)$. For each $D\in\{S,T\}$, the given measurable spaces, joint law $P_D$, measurable predictor $h$, and product-measurable loss $\ell$ form a supervised prediction problem with predictor class $\{h\}$. Since $h\in\{h\}$, the hypotheses of [F4] hold and $g_h$ is product-measurable. It is nonnegative, so both integrals in the claim are defined as extended nonnegative integrals.

By [F1] and [F2], the covariate-shift hypotheses hold and $w$ is an available input-marginal density. The joint-law lemma [F3] identifies the joint density as $r(x,y)=w(x)$. Apply [F5] to $g_h$ to obtain $\int g_h\,dP_T=\int g_h r\,dP_S=\int w(x)\ell(h(x),y)\,dP_S$. The assumed integrability makes this common value finite, proving the stated identity.

Let $(\mathsf X,\Sigma_X)$, $(\mathsf Y,\Sigma_Y)$, and $(\mathsf A,\Sigma_A)$ be nonempty measurable spaces. A **source/target pair of joint laws** consists of probability measures $P_S$ and $P_T$ on $(\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y,\Sigma_X\otimes\Sigma_Y)$. For $D\in\{S,T\}$, its input marginal is the probability measure $\mu_D$ on $(\mathsf X,\Sigma_X)$ defined by $\mu_D(A)=P_D(A\times\mathsf Y)$. If $h:\mathsf X\to\mathsf A$ is measurable and $\ell:\mathsf A\times\mathsf Y\to[0,+\infty]$ is product-measurable, then $(x,y)\mapsto(h(x),y)$ is measurable: the preimage of a measurable rectangle $U\times V$ is $h^{-1}(U)\times V$, and such rectangles generate the product sigma-algebra. Taking preimages once more shows that $(x,y)\mapsto\ell(h(x),y)$ is measurable. The domain risk is the extended nonnegative integral
$$R_D(h):=\int_{\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y}\ell(h(x),y)\,P_D(d(x,y)).$$

A **conditional label kernel** for $P_D$ is a specified probability kernel $K_D$ from $(\mathsf X,\Sigma_X)$ to $(\mathsf Y,\Sigma_Y)$ such that, for every nonnegative product-measurable $g:\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y\to[0,+\infty]$,
$$\int g(x,y)\,P_D(d(x,y))=\int_{\mathsf X}\left(\int_{\mathsf Y}g(x,y)\,K_D(x,dy)\right)\mu_D(dx).$$
The pair is under **covariate shift** when conditional label kernels $K_S,K_T$ are supplied, there is a measurable set $N$ with $\mu_T(N)=0$ such that $K_S(x,\cdot)=K_T(x,\cdot)$ as probability measures for every $x\notin N$, and $\mu_T\ll\mu_S$. No existence of conditional kernels is asserted by this definition.

Let $(\mathsf X,\Sigma_X)$ be a measurable space, equip $\{0,1\}$ with its discrete sigma-algebra, let $\mu_S$ and $\mu_T$ be probability measures on $\mathsf X$, and let $\mathcal H$ be a nonempty class of measurable classifiers $h:\mathsf X\to\{0,1\}$. For $h,h'\in\mathcal H$, define their measurable disagreement set by
$$A_{h,h'}:=\bigl(h^{-1}(\{0\})\cap h'^{-1}(\{1\})\bigr)\cup\bigl(h^{-1}(\{1\})\cap h'^{-1}(\{0\})\bigr).$$
The **$\mathcal H\Delta\mathcal H$ divergence** of the two input laws is
$$d_{\mathcal H\Delta\mathcal H}(\mu_S,\mu_T):=2\sup_{h,h'\in\mathcal H}\left|\mu_S(A_{h,h'})-\mu_T(A_{h,h'})\right|\in[0,2].$$

A **supervised prediction problem** consists of nonempty measurable spaces $(\mathsf X,\Sigma_X)$ of instances, $(\mathsf Y,\Sigma_Y)$ of labels, and $(\mathsf A,\Sigma_A)$ of prediction actions; the product measurable space $(\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y,\Sigma_X\otimes\Sigma_Y)$; a probability measure $P$ on that product; a nonempty class $\mathcal F$ of measurable predictors $f:\mathsf X\to\mathsf A$; and a loss $\ell:\mathsf A\times\mathsf Y\to[0,+\infty]$ that is measurable with respect to $\Sigma_A\otimes\Sigma_Y$. The law $P$ need not be supported on a deterministic labeling function, and this definition imposes no assumption that sample observations be independent or share a common law.

Let $(\mathsf X,\Sigma_X)$ and $(\mathsf Y,\Sigma_Y)$ be measurable spaces, let $P$ and $Q$ be probability measures on $\mathsf X$ (in particular, source and target input marginals), and let $\mathcal H$ be a nonempty class of measurable functions $h:\mathsf X\to\mathsf Y$. Let $L:\mathsf Y\times\mathsf Y\to[0,+\infty]$ be product-measurable. For $h,h'\in\mathcal H$, the map $x\mapsto(h'(x),h(x))$ is measurable because the preimage of each measurable rectangle $A\times B$ is $h'^{-1}(A)\cap h^{-1}(B)$ and such rectangles generate the product sigma-algebra; composing with $L$ shows that $x\mapsto L(h'(x),h(x))$ is measurable. Assume that, for every $h,h'\in\mathcal H$, the two integrals below are finite, and define
$$L_P(h',h):=\int_{\mathsf X}L(h'(x),h(x))\,P(dx),\qquad L_Q(h',h):=\int_{\mathsf X}L(h'(x),h(x))\,Q(dx).$$
The **$L$-discrepancy** between $P$ and $Q$ over $\mathcal H$ is the extended nonnegative number
$$\operatorname{disc}_L(P,Q):=\sup_{h,h'\in\mathcal H}\left|L_P(h',h)-L_Q(h',h)\right|\in[0,+\infty].$$
The supremum need not be attained.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ and $(Y,\mathcal{B})$ be measurable spaces
([[def-measurable-space]]). A function $f : X \to Y$ is **measurable** when

$$f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \qquad \text{for every } B \in \mathcal{B}.$$

Equivalently, the family

$$\mathcal{C}_f := \{\, B \subseteq Y : f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \,\}$$

is a sigma-algebra on $Y$ containing $\mathcal{B}$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

derivations.claim: For measurable $g_1,g_2:\mathsf X\to\mathsf Y$, let $G(x)=(g_1(x),g_2(x))$. For each measurable rectangle $A\times B$, $G^{-1}(A\times B)=g_1^{-1}(A)\cap g_2^{-1}(B)\in\Sigma_X$, so $G$ is measurable into $\Sigma_Y\otimes\Sigma_Y$ by [F3] and [F4]. For each Borel $C\subseteq[0,+\infty]$, $(L\circ G)^{-1}(C)=G^{-1}(L^{-1}(C))\in\Sigma_X$; hence all displayed loss integrands are measurable. Pairwise integrals with both arguments in $\mathcal H$ are finite by [F2], while integrals involving $f_P$ or $f_Q$ are defined extended nonnegative values.
Fix $h\in\mathcal H$. Applying the triangle inequality twice, pointwise and then integrating under $P$, gives $L_P(h,f_P)\le L_P(h,h_Q^*)+L_P(h_Q^*,h_P^*)+L_P(h_P^*,f_P)$.

A second triangle inequality gives $L_P(h,f_P)\le L_P(h,h_P^*)+L_P(h_P^*,f_P)$. Apply [F2] to the first term, then use the triangle inequality under $Q$ to obtain $L_Q(h,h_P^*)\le L_Q(h,h_Q^*)+L_Q(h_Q^*,h_P^*)$. Hence $L_P(h,f_P)\le L_P(h_P^*,f_P)+L_Q(h,h_Q^*)+\operatorname{disc}_L(P,Q)+L_Q(h_Q^*,h_P^*)$.
By [F2], $L_P(h,h_Q^*)\le L_Q(h,h_Q^*)+\operatorname{disc}_L(P,Q)$. Substitution in step 1.2 yields $L_P(h,f_P)\le L_P(h_P^*,f_P)+L_Q(h,h_Q^*)+\operatorname{disc}_L(P,Q)+L_P(h_Q^*,h_P^*)$.
The bounds in steps 2.1 and 1.3 have the same terms except for the final cross-domain term. Taking the smaller of those terms proves the stated minimum bound.

derivations.claim: For $N\ge1$, $\sum_{n=1}^N2^{-n}=1-2^{-N}$, so the source masses sum to $1$. Also $\sum_{n=1}^N n2^{-n}=2-(N+2)2^{-N}$: this holds at $N=1$, and adding $(N+1)2^{-(N+1)}$ proves the formula at $N+1$. Since $N2^{-N}\to0$, the target masses sum to $\frac12\sum_{n\ge1}n2^{-n}=1$.

Every source atom has positive mass, so the only $\mu_S$-null set is empty and $\mu_T\ll\mu_S$. The atomwise ratios satisfy $\mu_T(\{n\})/\mu_S(\{n\})=n/2$, hence $w(n)=n/2$ is a density and $\sup_n w(n)=+\infty$. The two conditional label kernels are identical.
The loss of $h(n)=1$ against label $0$ is $1$, hence $R_T(h)=1$. Its weighted source risk is $\sum_{n\ge1}2^{-n}(n/2)=1$ by step 1.1; thus it is finite and equals the target risk.

derivations.claim: The two input marginals are identical, so every disagreement event has the same probability under them; [F2] gives $d_{\mathcal H\Delta\mathcal H}(\mu_S,\mu_T)=0$.
